The following examples demonstrate these contrasts on two syllable words. /'ema/ I will see — /e'ma/ they; /'uta/ they did — /u'ta/ he is doing; /'ina/ white — /i'na/ fire; /'yana/ we are — /ya'na/ spear it!

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Yareba has an empty rule field and there are no existing statements, so this statement fills the gap rather than agreeing or contradicting: contrastive stress limited to the first two syllables of the stem. Quote verified against the page scan (scanned/), not only the scanned text, which garbles the end of the first sentence.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is contrastive (phonemic) and falls on either the first or the second syllable of the stem; minimal pairs of disyllables differ only in stress position, so placement is not predictable from syllable count or shape (all syllables are open CV/CVV/V/VV).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the section is four lines plus four minimal pairs, restricted to stems (affixed forms not discussed).
new_statements.identity_note: Weimer & Weimer 1972 was collected in the village of Bibira, middle Musa Valley (Yareba proper; the 1973 NT is labelled 'Middle Musa dialect' in Glottolog). The two unread SIL manuscripts cover the whole Yareban family (Yareba, Aga Bereho/Bariji, Aneme Wake, Moikodi, Sirio/Nawaru per the Glottolog hh records), so if read later any stress statement in them must be checked for which language it refers to.

new_statements.quote: [p. 5, about Oiso, a Maria dialect:] The sound system of Oiso remains largely unanalyzed. It appears to be a fairly complex system of stress, possible tone, long and short vowels, glottal and nasal. ... We will make no attempt to record, what we think may be tone, but may well turn out to be a complex stress system. An attempt will be made, however, to mark stress. [p. 6, Word List, Yareba column, stress marked with acutes:] 1. hair fóúma íji 2. head kofíri 3. mouth bebétu 4. nose ibó 5. neck ubíri 6. eye díti 7. belly desíni 8. skin ófe 9. knee yajígo 10. man éme ... 18. he walks inárasu ... 21. big deráwere 22. small kíkiratu 23. fire iná 24. smoke gibóri

It appears to be a fairly complex system of stress, possible tone, long and short vowels, glottal and nasal.. We will make no attempt to record, what we think may be tone, but may well turn out to be a complex stress system. An attempt will be made, however, to mark stress.'); the compiler ellipsis skips the Oiso consonant/diphthong remarks, correctly. p. 6 word list verified…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Yareba (catalog-all-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so nothing to agree or disagree with; this work contributes stress-marked Yareba forms (pp. 6-11) showing variable placement, but no prose rule. The p. 5 stress/tone passage is not about Yareba (Oiso = Maria). The variable marking is consistent with the on-disk Weimer & Weimer 1972 Te Reo 15 'Yareba phonemes' §3 (p. 56: 'Contrastive stress occurs on the first or second syllable of stems', read from the the compilation's scanned file), which is not one of this item's listed works. download history: live sil.org PDF not reachable by automated download on the third automated download…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for Yareba word stress is stated anywhere in the manuscript: §2 (vowels, diphthongs) and §3 (consonants, contrastive pairs, interpretation) contain no stress or prosody subsection, and the only prose about stress/tone (p. 5) concerns Oiso, a dialect of Maria, not a Yareban language. However, the 140-item comparative word list (pp. 6-11) marks stress with an acute accent on every form in all six columns. In the Yareba column the marked syllable varies from word to word: penult most often (kofíri, bebétu, ubíri, desíni, yajígo, gasíra, yaubínu, gebíro, gibóri), but also antepenult/initial in longer words (inárasu, deráwere, kíkiratu, áínibinu) and final (ibó, iná). As data this shows stress position is not fixed, consistent with contrastive/lexical stress, but the authors do not say so here.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None discussed; a few forms carry two acutes on a vowel sequence (fóúma, áínibinu), apparently marking a stressed diphthong rather than secondary stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Both manuscripts compare five Yareban-family languages: Yareba (Middle Musa, c. 750 speakers), Sirio (Namudi, Sibia), Moixodi/Moikodi (= Dutton's Doriri), Aneme Wake (Jari, Safia No. 2; Dutton groups it with Abia) and Aga Bereho (= Dutton's Bariji); Abia/Abie data were not collected. The 1977 MS also includes a word list and text for Oiso, a Northern-Province dialect of the Maria language (not Yareban), and its p. 5 remarks on 'a fairly complex system of stress, possible tone' refer to Oiso only. The Yareba column of the word list is the variety relevant to yare1248.

sources.note: Verb-morphology paper only (primary/secondary/tertiary/complex verbs, class markers, aspect, tense, mood, enclitics). No mention of stress, accent, pitch or tone anywhere in the 13 pages (pp. 58-70); no stress marks in the phonemic transcriptions. Footnote 1 defers phonology to a companion paper in the same volume (Te Reo 15, pp. 52-57), which is the item to download for the stress question. Catalog entry (classification lexical, rule empty, no-tone per Maddieson 2013, from Weimer & Weimer 1975) is neither confirmed nor contradicted.
